Content:
Suppose that we want to find

Content:
[MATH: {\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \frac {\sin x}{x} }.]

Content:
If we try to plug in [MATH: x=0,] we get the indeterminate form [MATH: \dfrac{0}{0}.] So what can we do?

Content:
Fortunately, we can find this limit using L'Hopital's Rule, which states that if [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = 0] and [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = 0,] then

Content:
[MATH: \
\lim_{x\to a} \dfrac {f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x\to a} \frac {f'(x)}{g'(x)},]
provided that [MATH: f] and [MATH: g] are both differentiable at [MATH: x=a,] and that [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to a} \dfrac {f'(x)}{g'(x)}] exists.

Content:
So, by applying L'Hopital's rule to our limit, we get

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac {\sin x}{x} &= \lim_{x\to0} \dfrac {[\sin x]'}{[x]'}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac {\cos x}{1}\[5pt]
&= \cos 0\[5pt]
&= 1.
}]

sections.normalized_html: Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\rightarrow 3}\dfrac{x^3-27}{x-3}].

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Note that plugging in [MATH: x=3] gives the indeterminate form [MATH: \dfrac{0}{0}.] However, we can use L'Hopital's rule to find this limit:

[MATH: \eqalign{ \lim_{x\to 3} \dfrac {x^3-27}{x-3} &= \lim_{x\to3} \dfrac {[x^3-27]'}{[x-3]'}\[5pt] &= \lim_{x\to 3} \dfrac {3x^2}{1}\[5pt] &= 3(3)^2\[5pt] &= 27 }]

items.title: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \, \frac {\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2}.]
sections.readable_text: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \, \frac {\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If we plug in [MATH: x=0] we get the indeterminate form [MATH: \dfrac{0}{0},] so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

[MATH: \eqalign{ \lim_{x\to0} \dfrac{\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2} &= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac {\left[\sin^2 (2x)\right]'}{[x^2]'}\[5pt] &= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{2\cdot \sin (2x) \cdot\cos (2x)\cdot 2}{2x}\[5pt] &= \lim_{x\to 0}{2\cos (2x)} \cdot \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt] &= 2\cos(2\cdot 0)\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt] &= 2\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x} }] This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form [MATH: \dfrac{0}{0}.] But that's okay, because we can just apply L'Hopital's rule again! We get [MATH: \eqalign{ \lim_{x\to0} \dfrac{\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2} &= 2\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt] &= 2\lim_{x\to0} \dfrac {[\sin (2x)]'}{[x]'}\[5pt] &= 2\lim_{x\to0} \dfrac {2\cos (2x)}{1}\[5pt] &= 4\cos(2\cdot 0)\ &=4. }]

items.readable_text:
Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \, \frac {\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If we plug in [MATH: x=0] we get the indeterminate form [MATH: \dfrac{0}{0},] so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

[MATH: \eqalign{
\lim_{x\to0} \dfrac{\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2} &= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac {\left[\sin^2 (2x)\right]'}{[x^2]'}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{2\cdot \sin (2x) \cdot\cos (2x)\cdot 2}{2x}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}{2\cos (2x)} \cdot \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt]
&= 2\cos(2\cdot 0)\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt]
&= 2\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}
}]
This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form [MATH: \dfrac{0}{0}.] But that's okay, because we can just apply L'Hopital's rule again! We get
[MATH: \eqalign{
\lim_{x\to0} \dfrac{\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2} &= 2\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt]
&= 2\lim_{x\to0} \dfrac {[\sin (2x)]'}{[x]'}\[5pt]
&= 2\lim_{x\to0} \dfrac {2\cos (2x)}{1}\[5pt]
&= 4\cos(2\cdot 0)\
&=4.
}]

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)} .]
sections.readable_text: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)} .]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \ln\left(x^2\right) = -\infty] and [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{2}{x^2} = \infty] respectively, so we have the case [MATH: \dfrac{-\infty}{\infty}].

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

[MATH: \eqalign{ \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)} &= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{[\ln\left(x^2\right)]'}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)'}\[5pt] &= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\left(1/x^2\right)\cdot 2x}{-\left({4}/{x^3}\right)}\[5pt] &= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{x^{-2} \cdot 2x}{-4x^{-3} }\[5pt] &= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{2x^{-1}}{-4x^{-3} }\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \lim_{x\to 0} {x^2}\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 0\[5pt] &= 0. }]

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

[MATH: \eqalign{
\lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)} &= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{[\ln\left(x^2\right)]'}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)'}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\left(1/x^2\right)\cdot 2x}{-\left({4}/{x^3}\right)}\[5pt]

}]

In this lesson, we started out with a special case of L'Hopital's rule (the case of [MATH: \dfrac{0}{0}] as [MATH: x \to a]) and gradually introduced more cases. In closing, we will state the full version of L'Hopital's rule.

Content:
Suppose that
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to a} \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \dfrac{0}{0} \quad \textrm{or} \quad \lim\limits_{x \to a} \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \dfrac{\pm \infty}{\pm \infty},]
where [MATH: a] is any real number, or [MATH: \pm \infty.] Then we have
[MATH: \lim_{x\to a} \dfrac {f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x\to a} \frac {f'(x)}{g'(x)},]
provided that the following conditions are met:

Content:
- If [MATH: a] is a real number, and [MATH: f] and [MATH: g] are both differentiable at [MATH: x=a,] then the limit [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to a} \frac {f'(x)}{g'(x)}] exists.
- If [MATH: a] is [MATH: \pm \infty,] and [MATH: f] and [MATH: g] are both differentiable for all sufficiently large [MATH: x,] then the limit [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\to \pm\infty} \frac {f'(x)}{g'(x)}] exists.

Content:
When working with familiar functions like polynomials, trigonometric functions, exponential functions, logarithmic functions, etc, it's safe to assume that these conditions are met.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that we want to find

Content:
[MATH: {\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \frac {\sin x}{x} }.]

Content:
If we try to plug in [MATH: x=0,] we get the indeterminate form [MATH: \dfrac{0}{0}.] So what can we do?

Content:
Fortunately, we can find this limit using L'Hopital's Rule, which states that if [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = 0] and [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = 0,] then

Content:
[MATH: \
\lim_{x\to a} \dfrac {f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x\to a} \frac {f'(x)}{g'(x)},]
provided that [MATH: f] and [MATH: g] are both differentiable at [MATH: x=a,] and that [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to a} \dfrac {f'(x)}{g'(x)}] exists.

Content:
So, by applying L'Hopital's rule to our limit, we get

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac {\sin x}{x} &= \lim_{x\to0} \dfrac {[\sin x]'}{[x]'}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac {\cos x}{1}\[5pt]
&= \cos 0\[5pt]
&= 1.
}]

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\rightarrow 3}\dfrac{x^3-27}{x-3}].

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Note that plugging in [MATH: x=3] gives the indeterminate form [MATH: \dfrac{0}{0}.] However, we can use L'Hopital's rule to find this limit:

[MATH: \eqalign{
\lim_{x\to 3} \dfrac {x^3-27}{x-3}
&= \lim_{x\to3} \dfrac {[x^3-27]'}{[x-3]'}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 3} \dfrac {3x^2}{1}\[5pt]
&= 3(3)^2\[5pt]
&= 27
}]

Item 5 — Example: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \, \frac {\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If we plug in [MATH: x=0] we get the indeterminate form [MATH: \dfrac{0}{0},] so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

[MATH: \eqalign{
\lim_{x\to0} \dfrac{\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2} &= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac {\left[\sin^2 (2x)\right]'}{[x^2]'}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{2\cdot \sin (2x) \cdot\cos (2x)\cdot 2}{2x}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}{2\cos (2x)} \cdot \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt]
&= 2\cos(2\cdot 0)\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt]
&= 2\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}
}]
This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form [MATH: \dfrac{0}{0}.] But that's okay, because we can just apply L'Hopital's rule again! We get
[MATH: \eqalign{
\lim_{x\to0} \dfrac{\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2} &= 2\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt]
&= 2\lim_{x\to0} \dfrac {[\sin (2x)]'}{[x]'}\[5pt]
&= 2\lim_{x\to0} \dfrac {2\cos (2x)}{1}\[5pt]
&= 4\cos(2\cdot 0)\
&=4.
}]

Item 8 — Tutorial: L'Hopital's Rule for the Case of Infinity Divided by Infinity

Content:
We can also use L'Hopital's rule to deal with the indeterminate form [MATH: \dfrac{\infty}{\infty}]. In this case, L'Hopital's rule states that if [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = \pm\infty] and [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = \pm\infty,] then

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to a} \dfrac {f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x\to a} \frac {f'(x)}{g'(x)},]

Content:
provided that [MATH: f] and [MATH: g] are both differentiable at [MATH: x=a,] and the limit [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to a} \frac {f'(x)}{g'(x)}] exists.

Item 9 — Example: Calculating an Indeterminate Limit of the Form Infinity Divided by Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)} .]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are
[MATH: \displaystyle
\lim_{x\to 0} \ln\left(x^2\right) = -\infty] and [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{2}{x^2} = \infty] respectively,
so we have the case [MATH: \dfrac{-\infty}{\infty}].

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

[MATH: \eqalign{
\lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)} &= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{[\ln\left(x^2\right)]'}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)'}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\left(1/x^2\right)\cdot 2x}{-\left({4}/{x^3}\right)}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{x^{-2} \cdot 2x}{-4x^{-3} }\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{2x^{-1}}{-4x^{-3} }\[5pt]
&= -\dfrac{1}{2} \lim_{x\to 0} {x^2}\[5pt]
&= -\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 0\[5pt]
&= 0.
}]

Item 12 — Tutorial: L'Hopital's Rule for Limits at Positive or Negative Infinity

Content:
L'Hopital's rule can be extended to the case in which the limit is taken as [MATH: x\rightarrow \pm\infty.] In this case, L'Hopital's rule states that if either

Content:
- [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty}f(x) = \pm \infty] and [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty }g(x) = \pm \infty,] or
- [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty}f(x) = 0] and [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\rightarrow \pm\infty }g(x) = 0,]

Content:
then

Content:
[MATH: \
\lim_{x\to \pm\infty} \dfrac {f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x\to \pm\infty} \frac {f'(x)}{g'(x)},]
provided that [MATH: f] and [MATH: g] are both differentiable for all sufficiently large [MATH: x,] and the limit [MATH: \displaystyle\lim_{x\to \pm\infty} \frac {f'(x)}{g'(x)}] exists.

Item 13 — Example: Calculating a Limit at Positive or Negative Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: {\displaystyle \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac {x^6}{5x^6-4} }.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type [MATH: \dfrac{\infty}{\infty},] so applying L'Hopital's rule yields
[MATH: \eqalign{
\lim_{x\to \infty} \dfrac {x^6}{5x^6-4} &= \lim_{x\to\infty} \dfrac {[x^6]'}{[5x^6-4]'}\
&= \lim_{x\to \infty} \dfrac {6x^5}{5(6x^5)-0}\
&= \lim_{x\to \infty} \dfrac {1}{5}\
&= \dfrac{1}{5}.
}]
